elements.char: Dosimetry models.
elements.label: text

elements.char: The primary inputs to the PBPK model are the rate of nicotine transfer to the tissues
elements.label: text

elements.char: at the absorption sites and duration of exposure. For oral products, nicotine is released from the product, mixed
elements.label: text

elements.char: with the saliva, partially transferred to the oral tissue. For inhalable vapor or aerosols, nicotine transfers to the
elements.label: text

elements.char: airway tissues via vapor phase and particulate phase in parallel. The physics associated with each and the corre-
elements.label: text

elements.char: sponding mathematical modeling for these products are different and hence require different dosimetry models.
elements.label: text

elements.char: The dosimetry models described below show how the nicotine transfer rate to the tissue is calculated for each
elements.label: text

elements.char: product category.

elements.char: Aerosol deposition model: dosimetry estimates for inhalable aerosols generated from use of ENDS and conventional
elements.label: text

elements.char: cigarette products.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Chemical constituents in aerosols delivered by ENDS and conventional cigarettes are pre-
elements.label: text

elements.char: sent both in vapor phase in air, as well as in the liquid phase as droplets. The partitioning between the two phases
elements.label: text

elements.char: depends on the volatility of constituent and what fraction of the constituents is bound in the liquid droplets.
elements.label: text

elements.char: This, along with the hygroscopicity of aerosol, as well as complex aerosol composition, makes the dynamics
elements.label: text

elements.char: of aerosol transport in the RT much more complex than the vapor phase alone. Furthermore, the aerosol can
elements.label: text

elements.char: deposit in different locations across the RT; starting from the BC down to the alveoli. Therefore, more complex
elements.label: text

elements.char: models are needed to predict the regional absorption of nicotine in the RT from products that generate inhalable
elements.label: text

elements.char: aerosols. Detailed descriptions of models for characterization of deposition of aerosol constituents in the RT are
elements.label: text

elements.char: beyond the scope of this article. Readers are referred to our prior
elements.label: text

elements.char: publications
elements.label: text

elements.char: for more details.
elements.label: text

elements.char: As an example of application of the aerosol deposition model, we used data from a clinical study sponsored
elements.label: text

elements.char: by Altria Client Services LLC and conducted by contract research organization Celerion, in compliance with
elements.label: text

elements.char: Good Clinical Practice principles. Subjects were instructed to take 10 puffs, each 5 s duration and 30 s puff
elements.label: text

elements.char: intervals on a cig-a-like ENDS device. Based on machine testing, this device delivered approximately 0.15 mg
elements.label: text

elements.char: nicotine in a 5 s puff. The distribution of nicotine deposition in the RT, employing the aerosol deposition model
elements.label: text

elements.char: described in our prior
elements.label: text

elements.char: publications
elements.label: text

elements.char: is shown in Fig. 2. Results show that for this use case, approximately 20%
elements.label: text

elements.char: of inhaled nicotine is absorbed in the BC, 25% in the URT, 50% in the LRT and 5% is exhaled. This distribution
elements.label: text

elements.char: varies considerably depending on the use topography and the pH of aerosol. The significance of pH is on the
elements.label: text

elements.char: fraction of free base nicotine and vapor-particle partitioning. More free base nicotine means more volatility,
elements.label: text

elements.char: hence more vapor phase.
elements.label: text

elements.char: For conventional cigarettes, 100% of inhaled nicotine is assumed to be retained in the body after each
elements.label: text

elements.char: puff
elements.label: text

elements.char: Furthermore, 95% of nicotine of the retained nicotine is assumed to be absorbed in the LRT and is transferred
elements.label: text

elements.char: instantly to the circulation system. The remaining 5% is assumed to be absorbed in the BC and the URT.

elements.char: Vapor absorption model: dosimetry estimates following use of products that generated inhalable nicotine vapors.
elements.label: text

elements.char: The
elements.label: text

elements.char: uptake of nicotine from products that deliver inhalable vapor follow a different mechanism compared to those
elements.label: text

elements.char: described earlier. Inhaled vapor is transferred from air to the RT surface. In general, vapor phase nicotine, upon
elements.label: text

elements.char: inhalation, is rapidly absorbed in the BC and URT. This is due to the rapid diffusion of vapors along the BC and
elements.label: text
